content:
An activity diary is a simple record of what you do each day and how your pain and energy feel. If you live with arthritis and frailty, it may help you notice patterns that are hard to notice otherwise, such as doing a lot on a good day and then needing several days to recover. This is often called boom and bust.

This guide explains how to keep a diary, what to look for, and how to use it to pace activity and set small goals. It is educational information, not a diagnosis.

Why keep a diary

A written record may help you notice patterns and explain them to your GP, physiotherapist or occupational therapist. A task followed by pain does not prove it caused the pain. Royal National Orthopaedic Hospital pacing advice describes breaking activities into manageable parts and balancing activity and rest. The Royal College of Occupational Therapists (RCOT) recommends pacing, planning and prioritising to manage energy. RCOT is a professional body, not the NHS.

How to keep it

  • Use a notebook, a printed table or a phone note, whichever is easiest for your hands.
  • Split each day into morning, afternoon and evening.
  • Write down the main activities and roughly how long each took.
  • If useful, score pain and energy from 0 to 10. Label each scale, for example 0 = no pain and 10 = worst pain; for energy, 0 = no energy and 10 = full energy. Use the same meaning each time.
  • Note sleep, rests, medicines taken and anything unusual, such as a flare or a bad night.
  • One to two weeks is a practical starting example, not a validated minimum or a reason to delay advice. Use a shorter record if that is all you can manage.

What to look for

  • Boom and bust: a busy day followed by one or more days of high pain or exhaustion.
  • Time of day: whether mornings are stiffest or evenings most tiring.
  • Possible patterns: tasks followed by symptoms, including symptoms later that day or the next day. Also record occasions when the same task is comfortable. A diary cannot establish a trigger or diagnose a condition.
  • Too little activity: long stretches sitting, which can lead to stiffness and weaker muscles.

Turning it into a plan

  • Break big tasks into smaller parts with rests in between.
  • Spread demanding jobs across the week.
  • With your therapist, identify a manageable starting amount of activity that fits your current symptoms, balance and other conditions. Do not test your maximum or force a bad-day target.
  • Once a routine is manageable, discuss whether a small change is appropriate and allow it to settle before another change. There is no automatic weekly increase. Reduce or adapt an activity if your plan or symptoms require it.
  • Plan rests before you are exhausted, not after.

How NICE guidance applies

NICE NG226, recommendations 1.3.1 to 1.3.3, supports tailored therapeutic exercise for osteoarthritis. NICE NG193, section 1.1, supports person-centred assessment and shared care planning for all chronic pain; its section 1.2 treatment recommendations are for chronic primary pain, not automatically every arthritis diagnosis. These recommendations do not validate this diary or prescribe a one-to-two-week recording period.

For people with several long-term conditions, including those with frailty, NICE NG56 recommends considering how conditions and treatment interact and agreeing individual goals. If falls are a concern, NICE NG249, recommendation 1.3.10, says falls-prevention exercise should be delivered by appropriately trained professionals, tailored to the person and reviewed regularly. A diary is not a frailty or falls assessment.

If you have ME/CFS, do not apply a generic activity-increase plan. NICE NG206, recommendations 1.11.13 and 1.11.14, requires flexible changes within energy limits and says not to offer programmes using fixed incremental increases. If activity causes delayed, disproportionate worsening or prolonged recovery, describe this to your clinician before trying to increase it.

Setting tiny goals

Choose a small goal that matters to you and is safe for your current abilities. It might be a short supported activity or part of a household task, rather than a standing or walking target that risks a fall. Agree changes with your therapist if you have frailty, falls or several conditions. Record what happened without treating an unfinished goal as failure. A setback may need rest, adaptation or medical review, not an automatic push to increase activity.

A blank sheet for flare notes

If you also want to record a flare, the blank daily log has space for notes to discuss with your healthcare team. It is not a replacement for the activity diary described above. The sheets do not send your entries to this website and are not a treatment plan.

Follow your existing care plan and the urgent-help advice in this guide. Do not delay medical help to complete a record.

Sharing it

  • Take the diary to GP, physiotherapy or rheumatology appointments.
  • A carer or family member can help fill it in if you want them involved and writing is painful. Include your own account wherever possible.

When to get help

  • Call 999 or go to A&E if someone suddenly becomes confused. Many causes need immediate assessment. Do not assume it is a urine infection, dementia or a medicine effect. Do not drive yourself to A&E; ask someone else to drive or call 999. Stay with the person and reassure them while help is arranged.
  • Call 999 for chest pain, severe breathing difficulty or stroke signs. After a fall, call 999 if you cannot get up or may have injured your head, back, neck or hip. NHS falls advice says not to try to lift another person yourself.
  • Ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111 for a sudden drop in mobility, sudden severe joint pain, new swelling, skin colour change or difficulty moving a joint. NHS septic arthritis guidance says fever is not always present. Do not wait for fever or finish a diary first.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

How long should I keep it?

One to two weeks is a practical starting example, not a diagnostic test or a required wait. A shorter record may still help a discussion. Ask for advice sooner if symptoms change, and restart a record only if it is useful to you.

Is resting always safer?

No. Too much rest can lead to stiffness and weaker muscles. The aim is a steady balance.

What if writing hurts my hands?

Use a voice note, a phone app, or ask someone to write it for you.
